title: A trispecific antibody engaging T cells with tumour and myeloid cells augments antitumour immunity
one_line: The authors built a trispecific antibody that simultaneously binds a tumour antigen, CD3 on T cells and a myeloid-cell target, showing that recruiting myeloid cells into the T-cell/tumour synapse augments antitumour immunity beyond a conventional bispecific T-cell engager.
key_claims: A single trispecific molecule can bridge three cell types — tumour, T cell and myeloid cell — rather than the two engaged by standard CD3 bispecifics.
Adding the myeloid-engaging arm improved antitumour activity relative to the matched bispecific T-cell engager control.
Myeloid-cell engagement is presented as a co-stimulatory/supportive mechanism that enhances T-cell-mediated tumour killing in the tumour microenvironment.
The design is proposed as a general format for overcoming myeloid-driven immunosuppression in solid tumours.
limitations: Show notes provide only the DOI, so specific antigen targets, affinities, formats and quantitative efficacy values are not captured here.
Effects demonstrated in preclinical models; no clinical data.
Trispecific engagement of myeloid cells raises cytokine-release and on-target/off-tumour safety questions not resolved by the episode material.
open_questions: Which arm's affinity dominates the therapeutic window, and does attenuating the CD3 arm preserve the myeloid benefit?
Does the trispecific outperform the bispecific in immunocompetent models with a fully human-like myeloid compartment?
What is the cytokine-release profile relative to the matched bispecific at equi-efficacious doses?
